9.6.1.en: No one expects that the sun will not rise at its appointed time, since the Lord set fixed laws for it. But if He wills, it does not rise. Once He commanded it to stand still to serve His people, and it stood still (Josh 10:12). What happened in the days of Joshua the son of Nun proclaims God's wonderful work through His servants, and as St. Athanasius the Apostolic says: [Though the sun stood still at Gibeon, and the moon in the valley of Ajalon, yet this work is not the work of the son of Nun, but the work of the Lord who heard the prayer, He who rebuked the sea, and on the Cross made the sun darken (Mt 27:45).]

9.6.2.en: Again God commanded the sun to go back, and it obeyed the divine command (2 Kgs 20:9). So also with the stars, He alone is able to seal them or hide them from our eyes.

9.6.3.en: God by His will preserves the order of the course of nature as an extension of the process of creation, and as a work of the divine providence.

9.7.0.en: Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea [8].

9.7.1.en: God, who created the universe, preserves the law of nature, so the heavens remain spread out, and without His providence their order would collapse. He treads the seas with His feet and prevents them from returning to "turn again to cover the earth" (Ps 104:9). He walks upon the raging waves, declaring that He alone calms all the waves of trials raging against us.

9.7.2.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that there is no point of comparison between what Moses the prophet did during the crossing of the Red Sea and the Lord Christ's walking on the water. What Moses did he did as a servant through prayer, but the Lord Christ did so with absolute authority. When the wind blew they crossed under Moses' leadership on dry ground in the midst of the sea (Ex 14:21), but the Lord Christ walked on the surface of the sea as upon a road, to bear witness to what is written in Scripture: [Who walks on the sea as on a pavement].

9.7.3.en: * "Which alone spreadeth out the heavens" [8] - by the heavens what does he indicate but the heavenly life itself of the preachers, of whom the psalmist said: [The heavens declare the glory of God] (Ps 19:1).

9.7.5.en: * The Gospel of the Lord teaches us that it was not the Father but the Son who walked on the sea when Peter asked Him, saying: "Lord, bid me come unto thee on the water" (Mt 28:14).

9.7.6.en: * It is the Lord who seals and numbers the host of the stars (Job 9:7)(g). He alone spreads out the heaven, and He walked on the sea as upon a pavement (Job 9:8; Mt 14:25).

9.7.7.en: When Peter saw Him walking, he said: "Lord... bid me come unto thee on the water" (Mt 14:28). The Lord commanded him, but he hesitated and nearly sank and perished among the waves, had the Lord not stretched out His right hand to him (Mt 14:29-31). The body staggered, and the right hand of the Lord rescued. And the Lord said to him: "O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" (Mt 14:31) It was faith that walked in the person of the Apostle, not the body.

9.7.8.en: St. Ambrose * Who could walk on the sea if not the Creator of the world?

9.7.9.en: Truly the Holy Spirit, who spoke very anciently through the blessed Job, said of Him: [Who alone spreads out the heavens, and walks on the sea as on the earth].

9.7.10.en: It was said of Him in the person of Wisdom: [I dwelt in high places, and my throne was in a cloudy pillar] (Sir 24:7).

9.7.11.en: Likewise David declared in the Psalm: [Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters] (Ps 19:77) Note also Habakkuk: "The overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice" (Hab 10:3).

9.8.0.en: Father Chromatius Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south [9].

9.8.1.en: He is the Creator of the groups of stars, and here three groups are mentioned on behalf of all: "Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades," and He still preserves them in existence and directs their movements, for the service of mankind.

9.8.2.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that when Scripture here mentions Arcturus, Orion and the Pleiades, it means all the stars and His divine providence over them. This is like when it refers to His care for the young ravens (Ps 147:9), it means all the birds.

9.8.3.en: "The chambers of the south," that is, the stars seen from the side of the South Pole and not seen by those in the northern hemisphere.

9.8.4.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these stars a symbolic meaning of the seven churches, which are the universal Church, which St. John the Beloved saw as seven lampstands. It enjoys the seven gifts of divine grace; its rays shine with the light of virtue issuing from the Truth.

9.8.5.en: * By Arcturus, Orion, Pleiades and the chambers of the south he indicates the whole group of the stars of the heavens and everything that is there... Job is surely speaking of every kind of miracle accomplished by God. In any case he speaks rather of the dispensations accomplished for our sake, for they are certainly divine, lofty dispensations that surpass nature. They are incomprehensible, because they are too high for a human spirit to reach. And they are profitable because God receives worship from the creatures here below, and from those who are on high, which are filled with wonderful works... John the Theologian has declared to us: "And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written" (Jn 21:25). Not only because they are above all number, but because His works are lofty, and the ears of this world are unable to receive them.

9.9.0.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number [10].

9.9.1.en: Here Job repeats literally what Eliphaz had said, [please refer to the commentary on Job 5:9].

9.10.0.en: Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not [11].

9.10.1.en: God's works are transcendent; He works with us and around us and within us without our seeing Him (Acts 17:23). Our limited perception is unable to know His movements for our sake, so it is difficult, indeed impossible, for us to evaluate His actions, even the apparent ones, because we do not perceive what is behind them. We have no right to comment on His actions, or to think that we are able to explain them.

9.10.2.en: * Since the human race was deprived of inner joy because of sin, it lost insight of mind, and cannot tell where these things are going.

9.10.4.en: * [When (God) rises above me I do not see Him, and when He passes by me I do not know this either]. God rises above each one of us, when He postpones the judgment upon us. And on the other hand He passes by us, that is, passes in our midst... In the first place we cannot see Him with the eyes of our body, and secondly we cannot reach Him with our spirit, for what constitutes Him is exceedingly subtle not only for the eyes but even for spirits.

9.10.5.en: * He passes through our minds, but it is clear that His passing was accomplished through our life, where He passed by way of the dispensation of His incarnation, His suffering on the Cross, and His glorious resurrection... And above all this, who can know how He was man and God (at the same time); how He suffered and destroyed suffering; how He tasted death as man, and as God subdued Hades and destroyed death (1 Cor 15:54; 2 Tim 1:10; 1 Pet 3:22).

9.10.6.en: He is the One who freed mankind from that curse and from the evil of sin (Rom 8:2), and no one could lighten the burdens that were upon us, from which He freed us.

9.10.7.en: No one can any more say to Him: "What doest thou?" or why do You justify sinners, and bring - under the blessing - him who was under the threat of the curse (Gal 3:13-14; Deut 21:23). He did this first as God, by the power that belongs to Him as God, working with authority, burying the debt of our sins in the earth (Col 2:14), therefore he adds: "He turns back His anger," that which was against us.

9.10.8.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this is the state of the person who feels isolated from God. He passed by him and granted him the experience of purity, but afterward he fell under the bitterness of the temptations of the flesh, which surround the mind and throng upon it, so that the inner eye becomes unclean, and consequently unable to see God. This is by God's permission so that the mind may be humbled and seek divine help.

9.10.9.en: * When the mind finds itself weak under temptation it turns to seek the help of the divine Being, and ceases entirely to depend on itself. And so it happens that He passes by, and the mind clings itself to God in the deepest way, by the very means by which it grieved over its fall and its distance from God.

9.10.10.en: Therefore God's entering and departing cannot be fully discovered by our faculties as long as the place of alternation of our state (from God's entering and departing) is hidden from our eyes. For example there is no definite assurance whether a particular trial is for testing virtue or is an instrument for our destruction.

9.10.11.en: As for gifts, we never perceive whether they are rewards for works we have done, or are support on man's way to his (heavenly) homeland.

9.10.13.en: * When the Apostle touched on the knowledge of divine matters - in his Epistle to the Corinthians - he affirmed that his knowledge - despite what he had received of it - is still limited and extremely scant. For he said: "And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know" (1 Cor 8:2).

9.10.14.en: He assured us that now we know in part, but the greater part of it we shall know in the age to come: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away" (1 Cor 13:9-10).

9.10.15.en: And when he wished to clarify the difference between our knowledge here and our knowledge in the other life he resorted to this illustration: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:11-12).

9.10.16.en: Have you perceived the extent of the difference between them? It is like the difference between the knowledge of a little child and that of a mature man, and like the difference between seeing in a mirror and looking face to face, for the mirror indicates a deep expression but in obscurity...! Why then do we not believe Paul's words: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20).

9.10.17.en: Consider how it befits us to submit to God's will in silence!

9.10.18.en: He undoubtedly does not mean by this saying that he wishes to deprive us of our will. Far be it! But he affirms that the inquirer ought to keep silent, like clay in the hand of the potter, neither resisting nor disputing. He mentioned the potter and the clay to remind us of our nature, for they are on one level as regards their existence (since the potter is created from dust) and yet the clay submits to the potter; what forgiveness then can man hope for when he recklessly dares to dispute the will of God who formed him, though the difference between him and Being itself is infinite?!

9.10.19.en: Remember, O man: who are you?

9.10.20.en: Are you not clay and dust and ashes?

9.10.22.en: Are you not grass? Are you not the flower of the grass?

9.10.23.en: Thus the prophets compete in drawing pictures before our eyes to express the truth of our existence. But God, whom you want to subject to your reckless curiosity, is not subject to death or change. He is eternal, without beginning or end, incomprehensible, beyond all understanding and all reason, indescribable and invisible! These attributes cannot be grasped by me and you, or even by the Apostles and prophets, nor even by the heavenly powers - despite their invisible purity and spirituality and their continual dwelling in heaven.

9.11.0.en: St. John Chrysostom If he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou? [12]

9.11.1.en: God is the One with authority; no creature has the right to review what He does. We place our trust in Him, and accept His will, even when it seems bitter to us. "If he taketh away" even our souls, who can resist Him, or enter into discussion with Him? "Who will say unto him, What doest thou?" or why do You do so? (Dan 4:35).

9.11.2.en: * [If He wills to destroy, who can turn Him back, and who will say to Him: What doest thou?]

9.11.3.en: "Who can turn Him back?" that is, who will rescue us? No one can say: "What doest thou?" First, no one dares to, and no one would be there, because the results bear their own testimony.

9.11.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The works of our Creator must always be honored without examination, for they will not be unjust.

9.11.5.en: For he who searches for the cause of His secret counsel is counted as nothing but a man's resistance to His counsel in arrogance.

9.11.6.en: When man cannot discover the motive of God's works we must keep silent in humility, submitting to His works, because the bodily senses are not at a level that can penetrate the secrets of His majesty...

9.11.7.en: Later Paul adds: "Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20)

9.11.9.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on Job's saying: "Who will say unto him, What doest thou?" saying that no one can resist the wrath of God. Yet Scripture gives us several examples of some men of God standing before the wrath of God.

9.11.10.en: Moses the prophet resisted the wrath of God when he stood interceding for the fallen people, saying: "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (Ex 32:32).

9.11.11.en: Also Moses asked Aaron to take a censer, and put fire in it from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly to the congregation, and make an atonement for them, "for there is wrath gone out from the LORD" (Num 16:46-48).

9.11.12.en: And Phinehas quenched the wrath of God when the people committed fornication with strange women, and he showed his zeal by thrusting the Israelite and the Midianite woman through the belly, so the plague was stayed from the children of Israel (Num 25:8).

9.11.13.en: And so David stood interceding for his people before the Lord to remove His wrath from them (2 Sam 24).

9.11.14.en: And the Truth demanded of us that we pray even for our enemies and persecutors (Mt 5:44).

9.11.15.en: Thus God shows the greatness of His surpassing love for man, for although no being can stand before the wrath of God, yet even in His wrath He declares His love, giving man an opportunity to break into the love of God by his humility and repentance and love for God and people and for the salvation of his soul; he asks mercy for himself and intercedes for his brethren.

9.11.16.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh presents us with a wonderful picture of resisting the wrath of God, namely by repentance:

9.11.17.en: * Jonah said: There is no means of nullifying the wrath, for iniquity has entrenched itself and the overthrow has come to destroy you...

9.11.18.en: Distress has drawn near, and the fall is at the door.

9.11.19.en: The Lord sent me, that Mighty One who bears creation, to proclaim the overthrow with a voice of terror upon your walls...

9.11.20.en: These voices struck the king of Nineveh, and he was terrified when he heard the dreadful news. He feared Jonah more than ranks of mighty men. And the dreaded king humbled himself before a lowly man. He rose from his splendid throne. And the dreaded king humbled himself before a lowly man. He rose from his splendid throne and cast the crown from him, and put on sackcloth, and prepared himself for repentance...

9.11.21.en: He realized that this battle was not like the usual battles, so he gathered his people and urged them to strive. He gathered his soldiers and lined them up for supplication, and supplied the ranks of soldiers with prayers to fence the gates. He made men and women and children hold to fasting, each according to his strength, to line up for battle against the wrath.

9.11.22.en: The king said to his soldiers words like these: Gather together for supplication, for a new fight we enter, contrary to custom...

9.11.23.en: No son of a single day ceases from striving. A fierce battle, in which you will see no weariness. Infants nursing on milk join us here in the ranks and support us before evil comes upon us.

9.11.24.en: In this battle the boys are stronger than the men, and the children strive more easily than the mighty.

9.11.25.en: The children who have not sinned in this battle go out by the thousands and join us, for through them the struggle becomes better.

9.11.26.en: Behold, the Hebrew asserts and threatens our destruction, let us work lest he rejoice if we are defeated. He has not ceased calling for wrath upon our corruption. And we will not cease until we call for mercies for our salvation. The man sought to establish his word because he is a prophet; let him preach, and let us ask his Lord...

9.11.27.en: We return to his Lord, the One with authority, that He may not destroy us. He is a messenger who speaks what was told him. It is within his authority to preach, not to destroy, so let us not grieve. If the matter were in his (the prophet's) hand, he would overturn the city. Let us not tire, for destruction is in the hand of the Lord. It is not in the hand of the prophet to build and tear down as he threatens... But against his voice we awaken voices of repentance, and call with weeping, so that we silence the man and quiet him. Let us not ask him, for he will not obey us and stop his speech. Let us send the voices of our sufferings to the Most High, and He will save us.

9.11.28.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh God will not withdraw his anger.

9.12.0.en: The helpers of Rahab stoop under him [13].

9.12.1.en: When He is angry no one can turn Him back from His anger except His mercy and love. He crushes the proud who resist Him. And as it says in the Book of Zechariah, [Be silent, O all flesh, before the LORD] (Zech 2:13). Repentance with its sighs and tears and humility turns back the divine wrath.

9.12.2.en: * Repentance is a fire that consumes all human weakness, removes negligence and laziness and heaviness of the body, and gives the soul a wing with which to fly toward heaven, and shows it from this high summit the vanity of this present life.

9.12.3.en: He who does not rise to the observation post cannot take a true picture of the earth and its contents. For many things darken the field of vision, deafen the ears, and make the tongue falter. Therefore it befits man to pull himself away from this noise, and keep far from the smoke, and enter into solitude to find deep peace and calm and stillness together with enlightenment.

9.12.4.en: When the eyes are fixed on the love of God, and the ear no longer hears except His words as though a sweet spiritual symphony, the soul becomes (God's) captive and feels a loathing for food and sleep.

9.12.5.en: Truly the clamor of the world and material concerns slide over the soul but do not enter into it, and by the soul's rising thus it no longer cares about the cracking of earthly storms.

9.12.6.en: And just as the dwellers of the mountains no longer hear the sounds of the city nor see what goes on in it, but count all this like vague noise, so those who have left the world by their own will and set off flying in the heights of philosophy (wisdom) no longer perceive anything of the conditions of the world, for all their senses are directed toward heaven.

9.12.7.en: Therefore let us seek not only the solitude of the wilderness, but the solitude of inner desire. Let us hide on the highest summit of the soul where nothing earthly dwells.

9.12.8.en: The power of repentance is like a wind that drives away the dust and sweeps away passions faster than smoke.

9.12.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * What sins can repentance fail to wash away? What deep-rooted stains can such tears not wash? By Peter's threefold confession he wiped out his threefold denial.

9.12.10.en: St. Jerome * Prolonged prayer and abundant tears draw God to mercy.

9.12.11.en: * Weeping alone leads to blessed laughter.

9.12.12.en: * Jesus wished to show in Himself all the beatitudes, for He said: [Blessed are those who weep], and He Himself wept in order to lay the foundation of this beatitude well.

9.13.s.en: 3. His inability to contend with God

9.13.0.en: 14 How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him? 15 For though I were justified, I would not answer, but would implore mercy of my judge. 16 If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice. 17 He who crusheth me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause. 18 He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness. 19 If it be a matter of the strength of the strong, he saith: Here am I. And if it be a matter of judgment, he saith: Who will try me? 20 If I be justified, my mouth shall condemn me; and if I be perfect, he shall pronounce me guilty. 21 "I am perfect. I do not care for myself. I despise my life."

9.13.1.en: How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him [14].

9.13.2.en: Job stands in contrition before God, confessing that he is unable to enter into dialogue with Him. But as many see it, Job fixed his gaze on his weakness, and slid toward despair, instead of looking to God's surpassing mercies and His love for mankind, and forgot that the almighty God longs to enter into dialogue with His creature, and did not prevent Satan from conversing with Him, as we saw in the first two chapters of the book (1, 2).

9.13.3.en: * It is worth noting that this saint (Job) passed over to judging himself so that when God's judgment comes it finds nothing in him to lay hold of. He looks at his weakness and says: "How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him" [14]. For he does not rely on his own righteousness, but takes refuge in hope alone in appealing to God's compassion. Therefore he added: [Even if I had some righteousness I would not wish to answer, but would make supplication to my judge] [15]. And since he is aware of the appeal to God, he adds: [When I call He answers me, I believe that He does not hear my voice] [16]. Why does he diminish himself so... why is he terrified with such sorrowful doubt? His eyes are fixed on the dread of the Judge... and he shrinks before the power of the searching eye. For all that he does seems small to him.

9.14.0.en: For though I were justified, I would not answer, but would implore mercy of my judge [15].

9.14.1.en: Man may justify himself because he does not even know the truth of himself, and what is within him. He does not know the hidden faults that man himself may not perceive. This is what the Apostle Paul expressed by saying: "For I know nothing by myself," that is, he did not feel any evil dominating him, "yet am I not hereby justified" (1 Cor 4:4). So the Apostle feared that if he justified himself, hidden sins that he did not know would be revealed to him. This is what drove Job to ask mercy from the Judge, the Searcher of hearts, and to throw himself on His mercies and not on his own personal merits.

9.14.2.en: What occupies Job's mind is not to be justified in the eyes of people, for although they insult him and cast him to the ground, and crush him with their feet, the One who judges him is the merciful Judge, before whom he cannot be justified by himself, but seeks His mercy and divine tenderness.

9.14.3.en: * He says (Job to Bildad): You revile Job in vain. What do you gain by trampling the righteous with your feet? I postpone the judgment to God, taking refuge in His divine providence and tenderness. He does not listen to what is said about me without examining; He is not subject to what is said about me. God does not accuse Job as a sinner, nor does He even listen to it, for the following reason: even if I am righteous compared with those who are righteous, yet I need a kind of judgment of God concerning me and testimony from on high. If my life agrees with the divine truth of the Judge, then no one can nullify the power of this truth.

9.14.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * All human righteousness is not counted as righteousness if examined by exact judgments... As if he says plainly: Even if I need to grow in the practice of virtue, I would be advancing in life, not by my own merit, but by the forgiving grace of God. Therefore we must be fervent in prayer when we walk uprightly, so that all the ways of righteousness we walk may be seasoned with humility.

9.15.0.en: If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice [16].

9.15.1.en: Some interpret this statement: that since he believed, his prayers were heard, not for the sake of his prayer itself, but for the sake of the holy name of God in which he believed. "Not for your sakes do I this, saith the Lord GOD, be it known unto you" (Ezek 36:32).

9.15.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's speech here a living picture of the continual struggle in the life of the believer, for by grace he calls on God and God answers him, as his heart is inflamed with love for divine things, but in the midst of this wonderful loftiness temporal thoughts invade the mind, and the believer finds himself as one who has fallen, and thinks that God does not hear his voice.

9.15.3.en: * Often the mind is inflamed with the fire of divine love, and rises to see the heavenly things and the hidden mysteries. The mind moves to the heights, and is wounded by perfect love, and becomes a stranger to lower things; but afterward when it is struck by a sudden temptation the soul which God supported with a clear purpose bows down, and is wounded by a temptation that assails it. It stands bewildered, wavering between good and evil practices, and cannot tell which side is stronger.

9.15.4.en: It often happens that it stands amazed how it possesses the heavenly truths while it wrestles with evil thoughts. Again it needs to know how evil thoughts creep into it while the zeal of the Holy Spirit powerfully carries it to lofty things. These alternating movements (between heavenly thoughts and evil ones) are rightly seen by the psalmist when he declares: "They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths" (Ps 107:26)... The mind is terrified by these movements of its own, and by the things to which it is involuntarily subjected, until it thinks within itself that it is cast out and rejected.

9.16.0.en: He who crusheth me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause [17].

9.16.1.en: Job felt that he had not committed extraordinary sins, yet extraordinary calamities befell him, for the storms of trial blew, not to disturb him but to crush him. The calamities wounded him abundantly without cause.

9.16.2.en: Some commentators see that Job attacked divine justice by saying "without cause," but some see that Job was bewildered because he had not fallen into a flagrant transgression, nor committed a sin that in the eyes of people is a great crime.

9.16.3.en: * "He who crusheth me with a tempest" [17]... It is rightly called a "tempest," because it is announced by the disturbance of the elements. And as the psalmist testifies by saying: [Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him] (Ps 50:3). Another prophet also says: "The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm" (Nah 1:3). In this whirlwind the righteous man will not be broken, because he always fears and is afraid lest he be broken.

9.16.5.en: * Note in his words that he did not say: "He has never wounded me without cause," but "multiplieth my wounds without cause." For it is not because of the multitude of his sins that those many wounds came upon him, but to test his patience...

9.16.6.en: Again, he says: [His way have I kept, and not declined. From his commandments have I not departed] (Job 23:11-12). He keeps God's ways and did not turn aside from them, for he did not forget them, but was advancing running in them, although he is weak, and sometimes stumbles and falls. And yet he continues in the way, sinning less and less until he reaches the state of perfection, so that he no longer sins.

9.16.7.en: * He said this about the Jews who in their self-reliance despised grace, and did not believe in Christ, that he says that they wished to establish their own righteousness, this righteousness which is of the Law, not that they carry out the Law, but they establish their righteousness in the Law, when they reckon within themselves that they are able to carry out the Law by their own power, being ignorant of God's righteousness (Rom 10:3), not the righteousness that belongs to God but the righteousness that God grants to man.

9.17.0.en: St. Augustine He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness [18].

9.17.1.en: Every person is exposed to sufferings from time to time, but sufferings did not leave Job to breathe, nor did bitterness depart from him. And in all this he did not know what the cause was.

9.17.2.en: * "He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness" [18]. Often He allows trials to befall me, so that I cannot take my breath. For often the enemy brings torments upon me, [I am filled with bitterness]. Also my wife and my friends are the ones who make me out a fool by their reviling me and speaking with me spitefully. Therefore I feel that this comes upon me from God, who permits it to come upon me, although He is able to prevent it from me. And yet I will not cease to bear witness to God's justice and power (Ps 71:19). By His divine providence He keeps all things in His hand. No man of sound mind dares to slander His judgments, for they proceed from the righteous Almighty.

9.17.3.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem If it be a matter of the strength of the strong, he saith: Here am I.

9.17.4.en: And if it be a matter of judgment, he saith:

9.18.1.en: Job looks to God and sees Him, without dispute, as the Strong One, whom none can stand before. He speaks and it is done (Ezek 22:14). As for judgment, there is no higher authority, nor a supreme court that listens to the protest of a man; He is the Judge of all, above all creation.

9.18.2.en: * [Since He is strong, He judges; who then resists His judgment?] [19]... The sun proclaims Him as other creatures do, how great and mighty He is, and it cannot disobey His command (Ps 104:19). Likewise the moon proclaims Him as it grows (until the crescent becomes a full moon) and wanes (as it diminishes after its fullness) according to His law. The sea also proclaims Him, as it does not transgress the limits assigned to it, and the sand resists the violence of the waves.

9.18.3.en: This is the reason for which no one can resist His judgments and disobey them. In any case, if you are speaking of the judgments by which He judges mankind, who has the audacity to resist Him? If you speak of Abraham, he said of himself: "I am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27). And David in the same spirit said: "Mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me" (Ps 38:4).

9.19.0.en: He does not cease to sing with his harp what the famous Isaiah proclaims: [Woe is me, for I am a wretched man, of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people] who keep defiled teachings (cf. Isa 6:5). Therefore the wrestler adds: [If I appear righteous my mouth will be defiled] [20] How can this be? Listen: it is not easy for a person to be without blame in deeds and words. Therefore he rightly adds: [And if I appear perfect, I am surely a fool].

9.19.1.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Someone may say: What shall I do? How can I be light, when here I live in evils and iniquities?! And thereby despair and grief creep upon him, since we have no salvation without fellowship with God, and God is light and in Him is no darkness at all, and sin is darkness, so how am I to be cleansed from it?! The Apostle continues, saying: "and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." How great is this assurance that He has given us! By virtue of our being in this world in the midst of trials a man may stumble after his sins have been forgiven in Baptism, therefore we must do what we can, confessing our state as it is so that the Lord Christ may heal us by His blood.

9.19.2.en: St. Augustine If I be justified, my mouth shall condemn me?

9.19.3.en: And if I be perfect, he shall pronounce me guilty [20].

9.19.4.en: As for Job, if he justifies himself, his defense turns into iniquity, and he is judged by his words, for God knows the hidden things of the heart that man himself may not know. "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." If Job counts himself perfect, he counts this an accusation against God, and a guilt that he commits as a proud man ignorant of his depths.

9.19.5.en: * I glory that I am being saved, not because I am without sins, but because sins have been forgiven. I do not glory because I am useful or because someone is useful to me, but because Christ is my advocate (lawyer) before the Father, because the blood of Christ was shed for me.

9.19.6.en: St. Ambrose I am perfect. I do not care for myself.

9.20.1.en: Job looks to his old age and sees in himself that he is an old man who has no profit from the long years he has lived, for they have produced nothing! They are despised, fruitless years. These are the feelings of the man who looks at his life outside the circle of God's love and His grace, the Giver of fruit!

9.21.s.en: 4. We do not judge by appearance

9.21.0.en: 22 It is one. Therefore I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked. 23 If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent. 24 The earth is given into the hand of the wicked: he covereth the faces of the judges thereof; and if it be not he, then who?

9.21.2.en: Therefore I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked [22].

9.21.3.en: Job's friends insist that the righteous prosper in this world and are protected from trials, and if trials reach them they are soon removed from them. But the wicked fail, trials surround them in this world and crush them, and there is none to deliver. But Job affirms the opposite: some of the wicked may prosper and flourish in this world, while the righteous are exposed to successive trials. This is the main point of dispute in all the discussions between Job and his friends, whose aim is for the friends to affirm that Job is a wicked hypocrite, who bears the appearance of godliness and hides evils that anger God.

9.21.4.en: Job affirms here that temporal events are not the measure by which to recognize the truth of a man, whether righteous or wicked.

9.21.5.en: "It is one": calamities may befall the wicked as well as the righteous, and death comes upon these and those. "The sword devoureth one as well as another" (2 Sam 11:25). It devours Josiah the good king as it devours Ahab the wicked king. Thus we see that "He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked." The good and the wicked were sent together into the Babylonian captivity (Jer 24:5, 9).

9.21.6.en: * [It is one; I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked] [22]. This can be clarified in the following words: I said these words about myself, that even if I am perfect I do not appear perfect if examined closely, nor if I am wicked do I appear so if I remain hidden, withdrawn from the exact piercing examination. But the strict Judge, He perceives all things, and pierces the devices of the wicked in a wonderful way. In order to attain what is better He judges each according to his inclination.

9.21.8.en: * Are these not the utterances of the citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem:

9.21.9.en: [My tears have been my meat day and night] (Ps 42:3).

9.21.10.en: [All the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears] (Ps 6:6).

9.21.11.en: "My groaning is not hid from thee" (Ps 38:9).

9.21.13.en: Do not the children of God who groan, being burdened, not wish to be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life? Do not even those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan within themselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body? (Rom 23:8).

9.21.14.en: Did not the Apostle Paul himself, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, have all this when he was burdened and in continual sorrow of heart for his brethren the Israelites? But there will be no death in the City except when it is said: [O death, where is thy struggle? O death, where is thy sting? for the sting of death is sin].

9.22.0.en: St. Augustine If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent [23].

9.22.1.en: As the sword suddenly stretched out kills this one and that one; the wicked to his destruction, and the righteous for the proving of his faith. [That the proving of faith, though it is tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory] (1 Pet 1:7). For the innocent make light of death because it is a passing over into glory!

9.22.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on the phrase: [He laughs at the trial of the righteous] saying: [If He uses the expression "laughter" of God to mean His joy, it is said that He laughs at the trial of the righteous, since they seek Him zealously (in time of trial) and He rejoices in us tenderly, for our pain causes Him a kind of joy when we have holy desires to discipline ourselves out of our love for Him.]

9.22.3.en: * Paul says (2 Cor 4:17) that our present sorrows are light since they occur within the limits of a certain time and a particular place. In return for this light labor we acquire glory beyond all measure.

9.22.4.en: Ambrosiaster * Every trial is either a punishment for the wicked or a testing of the righteous... So peace and calm in times of contention can benefit the good while corrupting the wicked.

9.22.5.en: St. Augustine The earth is given into the hand of the wicked:

9.22.6.en: He covereth the faces of the judges thereof.

9.23.0.en: And if it be not he, then who? [24]

9.23.1.en: Often God allows the wicked to escape and even to rule over the earth; on the one hand the enemy does not complain that the righteous worship the Lord and fear Him to obtain temporal blessings and earthly success, and on the other hand God leaves the wicked in his freedom in case he repents of his deed if he touches God's love, or the cup of his evil is filled if he persists in his rebellion and stubbornness.

9.23.2.en: If the wicked enemy is called "the god of this world," we should not wonder if the wicked take over the earth and think they are successful and kings.

9.23.3.en: The earth is given into the hands of the wicked, and the righteous enjoy heaven, because the Heavenly One dwells in them.

9.23.4.en: [He covers the faces of the judges of the earth] while the righteous are subjected to injustice on earth and the wicked put on masks, so they appear as judges of the earth, as those who judge justly, though it is not so.

9.23.5.en: Despite presenting this truth, many see that Job's style carries a kind of murmuring: how does the Lord leave the wicked to prosper and dominate the earth, and appear as judges who judge the innocent.

9.23.6.en: With the presentation of an important principle with wisdom, Job's words could have comforted him inwardly, so that he would not care about his friends' accusations. But it seems that inner murmuring - as a human weakness - stirred up bitter feelings in him. For he saw that his days of prosperity had passed quickly, had fled from him, and no trace of them remained, so that he became as one who had never tasted good.

9.23.7.en: St. Augustine sees that the earth here indicates the body, for God may permit the body to be delivered for discipline into the hand of the wicked, or for testing and proving, but the soul of the righteous the enemy cannot approach.

9.23.8.en: What does the saying "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 24:9) mean but that, since the body was created from dust, God may permit our earthly bodies to be delivered to the wicked, but they have no authority over them except over the dust that is in them, but since it bears the new nature which is in the image of its Creator, and puts on the image of the second Adam who is from heaven, none of them has authority over it. St. Augustine sees that the divine Word Himself, when He became incarnate, took this earthly body and permitted it to be delivered to the wicked for trial and killing, so that we should not fear the wicked, but share with our Christ His sufferings and death in order to experience His resurrection and its glories.

9.23.9.en: * Often the righteous man is delivered into the hand of the wicked, not to honor the latter, but that the former may be tested, and although the wicked man comes to a stately death as it is written (Job 23:9), yet in the present time the righteous is an object of mockery, while the goodness of God and the great stores laid up for each are hidden.

9.23.10.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * What is the meaning of "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 9:24)? The body is delivered into the hands of persecutors, but God does not leave His righteous one there. From the captive body He brings out the soul that is not conquered.

9.23.11.en: * "The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him. The LORD will not leave him in his hand" (Ps 32:37-33). Why then did He leave the martyrs in the hands of the wicked? Why did they do to them whatever they wished (Mt 12:17)? They slaughtered some with the sword, and crucified some, and threw some to the beasts, and burned some with fire, and led some in chains, and destroyed them by ruinous schemes. Surely [the Lord did not forsake His saints](d) He does not leave them in their hands. Finally why did He leave His only-begotten Son in the hands of the wicked...? Hear what another book says prophesying about the sufferings of our Lord to come at the hands of the wicked: [The earth was given into the hands of the wicked] (Job 24:9)... He is speaking of the delivering of the body into the hands of the persecutors. But God did not leave "His chosen one" (Ps 10:16) there, for through the body that was captured, He led the soul that was not defeated.
